question: What is the main risk when a nurse gives an injection?

options.A: A sudden spike in blood pressure
options.B: Immediate muscle wasting at the site
options.D: A direct path for germs to enter the bloodstream

explanation: Breaking the skin lets microorganisms bypass your body's natural defenses and get straight into circulation. That's why being sterile is a big deal! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why is injection safety so important in Nigerian healthcare clinics?

options.A: Parenteral drugs are the only medications available in rural areas
options.B: Ministry rules ban oral painkillers completely
options.C: Injections are given frequently across almost all healthcare settings
options.D: Patients refuse to take oral medications everywhere

explanation: Since we give injections daily in clinics and wards, keeping safety standards high protects everyone from avoidable harm. You'll master this in no time! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h1)

question: What does 'injection safety' actually cover?

options.B: Preparation, giving the injection, and safe disposal of the device
options.C: Only how the syringe and needle are manufactured
options.D: Checking vital signs for twelve hours after

explanation: Injection safety covers the whole process—from drawing up the drug to safely dropping the needle in the bin. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h2)

question: A nurse prepares a sterile syringe, then tries to recap it using both hands before walking across the room. What safety rule was broken?

options.C: Provider protection and safe handling technique

explanation: Using two hands to recap a needle is a fast track to a needle-stick injury. Always protect yourself—never recap used needles! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h2)

question: According to WHO guidelines, what must be used for every single injection?

options.A: A single syringe shared among children
options.B: A new, sterile needle and syringe
options.C: A boiled metal needle and plastic barrel

explanation: Never reuse needles or syringes, not even on the same patient. A fresh, sterile set is required every single time. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h3)

question: Why does the WHO recommend engineered safety devices on needles?

options.A: To lower the cost of plastic syringe barrels
options.B: To actively prevent accidental needle-stick injuries to staff
options.C: To replace the need for hand washing
options.D: To make medications work faster in emergencies

explanation: Safety devices like retractable needles shield the sharp point after use, keeping healthcare workers safe from accidental pricks. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h3)

question: Which practice directly protects nurses from sharps injuries?

options.A: Recapping needles firmly using both hands
options.B: Storing used sharps in open cardboard boxes
options.C: Avoiding the manual recapping of used needles
options.D: Washing plastic syringes with bleach to reuse them

explanation: Most needle-stick injuries happen during recapping. Leaving used needles uncapped and dropping them straight into the safety box keeps your hands safe! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h4)

question: How do safe injection practices protect the wider community?

options.A: By lowering the market cost of imported drugs
options.B: By ensuring everyone gets annual vaccinations
options.C: By preventing hazardous medical waste from entering public dumps

explanation: Proper disposal keeps infectious needles out of public trash heaps where scavengers or children could get hurt. Community health starts with us! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h4)

question: What are the most common bloodborne infections spread by unsafe injections?

options.B: HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C

explanation: Sharing or reusing contaminated injection equipment is a major way these serious viral infections travel. Safety first! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h5)

question: A patient develops a painful, pus-filled swelling at an injection site a few days after getting a shot. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Rapid absorption of medication into deep bone tissue
options.B: A normal reaction to the drug
options.C: An allergic reaction to the plastic syringe
options.D: Bacterial contamination introduced during the injection

explanation: Painful abscesses usually happen when bacteria slip into the tissue because of a break in sterile technique. Clean technique prevents this! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h5)

question: What is considered the single most effective action in standard infection precautions?
explanation: Simple handwashing or using alcohol rub is your #1 defense against spreading germs. Never skip cleaning your hands! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h6)

question: While drawing up medication, you accidentally touch the sterile needle hub with your bare finger. What should you do?

options.A: Wipe the hub with alcohol and use it anyway
options.B: Discard the contaminated needle and syringe immediately
options.C: Flame the needle tip over a spirit lamp to sterilize it
options.D: Go ahead with the injection since skin is mostly clean

explanation: Once a sterile part is touched by unsterile skin, it's contaminated. Don't risk it—just grab a fresh needle and syringe! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h6)

question: When should a sharps container be closed and replaced?

options.A: When it reaches the fill line, usually three-quarters full
options.B: Once a month according to hospital policy
options.C: When it is packed completely to the brim
options.D: At the end of every single shift

explanation: Never overfill a sharps box! Once it's about 3/4 full, close it up and grab a new one to prevent accidental pokes. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h7)

question: Why should sharps containers be placed right next to where you give injections?

options.A: So patients can drop their own needles
options.B: To save space on the medication trolley
options.C: To comply with ward fire regulations
options.D: To eliminate carrying exposed needles across the room

explanation: Walking across a busy room with an uncovered needle is asking for an accident. Keep your sharps bin close at hand! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h7)
